sources.title: Chapter 10 - Principles of Pipelining (Basic Computer Architecture)
sources.channel: IIT Delhi, Prof. Smruti R. Sarangi (freely distributed book chapter)
sources.note: the whole 92-page chapter was read: the pipeline idea and its performance, the five stages, pipeline registers, data/control/structural hazards, software solutions, interlocks and bubbles, forwarding paths and conditions, interrupts, the performance equation, branch prediction, multiple issue and out-of-order execution

sourceLine: Throughput as the reciprocal of the cycle time, efficiency as speed-up over k, and the penalty growing with depth: Sarangi chapter 10, sections 10.9.2, 10.9.3 and 10.11.1 (English, read in full). The throughput, efficiency and depth-trade-off statements: DSWallah Learn 'Instruction Pipelining', romanised Hindi, translated (read in part).
title: Throughput, Efficiency and the Clock-rate Trade
unit: Instruction Pipelining: Stages, Timing and Speed-up
quickIdea: Throughput is instructions completed per unit time, which in the steady state is 1 / t_p. Anything that shortens the cycle time raises throughput even when the CPI and the instruction count do not change, which is why a percentage change in throughput is a percentage change in clock frequency.
remember: Steady-state throughput = 1 / t_p instructions per second; raising it means lowering max(stage delay) + latch delay.
For the same instruction stream, the percentage change in throughput equals the percentage change in clock frequency.
Efficiency = speed-up / k measures how much of the ideal k-fold gain a finite program realises; long programs approach 1.

Deeper pipelines lower t_p but raise the cycles lost per hazard, because the stall penalty grows with depth (Sarangi: 1 cycle for load-use and 2 for a taken branch at this depth, doubling when every stage is halved).
Splitting a stage is worth it only while that stage is the maximum; once another stage is, further splitting buys nothing.

example.prompt: A 4-stage pipeline has stage delays 800, 500, 400 and 300 ps. Its first stage is replaced by two stages of 600 and 350 ps. By what percentage does throughput rise?
example.work: Before: t_p = max(800, 500, 400, 300) = 800 ps, throughput 1/800. After: the stages are 600, 350, 500, 400, 300 ps, so t_p = 600 ps and throughput 1/600. The ratio is (1/600)/(1/800) = 800/600 = 4/3, so the increase is 33.33 percent.
example.answer: 33.33 percent, the accepted answer of GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 Q.32. Note that the cycle time fell by 25 percent but throughput rose by 33.33 percent: the two percentages are reciprocals, not the same number.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 Q.32 asks for the throughput increase from splitting a stage and expects 33.33; GATE CSE 2016 Set 2 Q.33 asks the same change expressed as a new clock frequency and expects 4 GHz. Both are one calculation: the new maximum stage delay.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: For the 2016 Set 1 pipeline, what is the throughput increase if the 800 ps stage is split into 400 + 400 ps instead of 600 + 350 ps?
variations.why: It tests whether the student recomputes the maximum instead of reusing the previous answer.
variations.answer: The stages become 400, 400, 500, 400, 300 ps, so t_p = 500 ps and throughput rises from 1/800 to 1/500, an increase of 60 percent. Splitting further helped only because 500 ps then became the limit, and no split of the first stage alone can now help.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A design halves every stage delay and doubles the stage count. What happens to throughput and what happens to the cost of a taken branch?
variations.why: It joins the two halves of the topic: the gain from frequency and the loss from penalty.
variations.answer: Throughput doubles, since the cycle time halves. The branch penalty doubles too, from 2 cycles to 4, because twice as many instructions are fetched before the branch resolves; a program with many taken branches therefore gains much less than 2x, which is the trade the chapter states as the reason pipeline depth is limited.

trap.what: Reporting the fall in cycle time as the rise in throughput.
trap.why: Throughput is the reciprocal of the period, so a 25 percent shorter period is a 33.33 percent higher rate. The two are not interchangeable.
trap.counterexample: 2016 Set 1 Q.32: (800 - 600)/800 = 25 percent is the reduction in cycle time; the accepted throughput increase is 33.33 percent.

check.question: A pipeline's cycle time falls from 5 ns to 4 ns with no change in CPI. What is the throughput increase?
check.answer: 25 percent: 1/4 against 1/5 is a ratio of 5/4.
check.explanation: The rate rises by the ratio of the old period to the new one, 5/4, which is a 25 percent increase - not the 20 percent by which the period fell.
